title: Why Databases Exist
description: Discover why flat files fall apart at scale, and how databases use tables, indexes, and transactions to keep your data safe and fast.

segments.text: Let's talk about one of the most fundamental building blocks of any system — databases. Before we get fancy, let's understand why they exist in the first place.
Imagine storing all your app's data in plain text files on disk. User data in users.txt, orders in orders.txt. Simple! This actually works fine when you're small.
But what happens when two users try to update the same file at the same time? Or when you need to find one order out of ten million? Things get ugly fast.
segments.thought_prompt: What problems would you face if your entire app's data lived in flat text files?

segments.text: Enter the database. It's a specialized piece of software designed to store, organize, retrieve, and protect data efficiently. Think of it as upgrading from a shoebox of receipts to a well-organized filing system.

Relational databases organize data into tables with rows and columns. A 'users' table has columns like id, name, and email. Each row is one user. The structure is defined upfront — that's your schema.
SQL is how you talk to the database. SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 42 — it's almost like English. You describe WHAT data you want, not HOW to get it. The database figures out the best way.

Without an index, finding one row means scanning every single row — like reading every book in a library to find one title. An index is like a card catalog: it tells you exactly where to look. Under the hood, most indexes use B-trees.

But indexes aren't free. Every index speeds up reads but slows down writes, because the index must be updated too. It's like maintaining a card catalog — adding a new book means updating the catalog as well.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose NOT to add an index to a column?

segments.text: Now for the real superpower of databases: ACID properties. These four guarantees are why banks trust databases with your money instead of text files.
Atomicity: all or nothing, no half-done operations. Consistency: data always follows the rules. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere. Durability: once committed, data survives crashes.
Every table needs a primary key — a column that uniquely identifies each row. It's like a Social Security number for your data. No two rows can share the same primary key, and it can never be null.

So databases solve the chaos of raw files with structure, fast lookups via indexes, a declarative query language in SQL, and bulletproof guarantees through ACID. This is the foundation we'll build on for everything from replication to sharding.
